clinicalPearls: A carpal boss is a firm bony prominence on the dorsum of the hand at the base of the second and third carpometacarpal joints, over the capitate-trapezoid-metacarpal junction.
It may represent a degenerative osteophyte or an accessory ossicle (os styloideum) and is frequently associated with dorsal carpometacarpal osteoarthritis.
The prominence becomes more visible with the wrist flexed and is hard and fixed, distinguishing it from the softer, mobile dorsal wrist ganglion.
A dorsal wrist ganglion may coexist and arise adjacent to the boss, complicating the clinical picture.
Many bosses are asymptomatic and found incidentally; symptomatic cases usually present with activity-related dorsal pain.
Extensor tendons may snap over the prominence, and a small overlying bursa or extensor tendon irritation can develop.
A dedicated carpal boss view, taken partially supinated, ulnar-deviated and slightly flexed, best profiles the ossicle.
reference.pathophysiology: The carpal boss is a bony excrescence at the second and third carpometacarpal joints, arising either as a degenerative osteophyte from the carpometacarpal articulation or from an unfused ossification centre (os styloideum) that persists as an accessory bone. Repetitive dorsal stress and osteoarthritic change at these tightly constrained carpometacarpal joints generate the prominence, which can mechanically irritate the overlying extensor tendons and a superficial bursa, producing localised dorsal pain.
additionalDifferentials: Anomalous extensor digitorum brevis manus muscle
additionalInvestigations: Focused dorsal hand radiographs including a partially supinated oblique carpal boss view
Lateral radiograph with the wrist slightly flexed to profile the prominence
CT to define an os styloideum and associated carpometacarpal arthritis
MRI if a soft-tissue mass or occult ganglion is suspected
Ultrasound to distinguish a solid boss from a cystic ganglion
Diagnostic local anaesthetic injection to confirm the pain source
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging or aggressive-looking bony lesion suggesting neoplasm
Features of inflammatory or crystal arthropathy
Extensor tendon attrition or rupture over the prominence
reference.prognosis: Most carpal bosses are benign and either asymptomatic or settle with activity modification; surgical excision relieves symptoms in refractory cases, though recurrence and residual dorsal ache can occur.
pitfalls: Confusing a hard, fixed carpal boss with a mobile dorsal ganglion.
Missing coexisting carpometacarpal osteoarthritis as the true pain source.
Using inadequate radiographic views that fail to demonstrate the ossicle.
Performing incomplete excision, which leads to symptomatic recurrence.
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
management: Activity modification and avoidance of repetitive dorsal wrist loading as first-line conservative management
Wrist splinting or bracing to rest the second and third carpometacarpal joints and relieve dorsal pain
Simple analgesia and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for symptomatic relief
Local corticosteroid injection into the associated bursa or joint for persistent symptoms
Surgical excision of the bony prominence, with carpometacarpal arthrodesis where there is established osteoarthritis, reserved for refractory cases
Counselling about the possibility of recurrence and residual dorsal ache after excision
Referral to hand surgery for persistent or diagnostically uncertain cases
